Tumultuous

/too-MUL-chuh-wus/ — stress on MUL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tumultuous describes something marked by great disorder, confusion, or emotional turmoil.

The crowd gave the returning astronauts a tumultuous welcome at the airport.

Worked Example

The college application season was a tumultuous time for Sarah—one day elated by an acceptance, the next devastated by a rejection.

Tumult (an uproar; a noisy commotion) + -uous (full of) = full of chaos and disorder. The base word 'tumult' is real English, so 'tumultuous' describes something that embodies that uproar. Sarah's emotional swings mirror the collision of hopes and fears—the turbulence that defines tumult.

How Tumultuous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

chaotic

chaotic: completely disordered, with no organization

turbulent

turbulent: full of violent, unsteady movement

stormy

stormy: wild and agitated, like bad weather

Antonyms

calm

calm: peaceful and free of disturbance

orderly

orderly: neatly arranged and well controlled

How Strong Is It? — noisy → rowdy → turbulent → tumultuous

noisy vs. tumultuous

noisy vs. tumultuous: A noisy hallway is loud, but a tumultuous one is in total uproar.

rowdy vs. tumultuous

rowdy vs. tumultuous: A rowdy crowd misbehaves, while a tumultuous crowd erupts into wild commotion.

turbulent vs. tumultuous

turbulent vs. tumultuous: A turbulent meeting has real conflict, but a tumultuous meeting collapses into complete chaos.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tumult

Root — tumult: an uproar; a noisy commotion (a real English word) (Latin (tumultus))

Suffix — -uous

Suffix — -uous: full of (a form of -ous) (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: The base is a real English word: tumult, a noisy uproar. Add -uous ('full of') and you get tumultuous — literally 'full of uproar,' perfect for a crowd that has erupted into commotion.

Use the root in a new word: tumult

Word Choice

neutral

Reach for tumultuous when describing situations marked by disorder, confusion, and emotional upheaval—crowds, receptions, elections, historical eras, or internal states. It works equally well for negative chaos (riots, conflict) and positive pandemonium (joyous crowds, enthusiastic audiences).
